svg.title: One feed file through the unattended nightly sync
svg.desc: The scheduled wrapper script takes the oldest file from the inbox and starts cedar-sync. Step 1, journal: if this exact content, identified by its SHA-256 hash, was completed before, the run is skipped with exit code 0. Step 2, parse and validate: a file that is not valid JSON or has more than 20,000 lines is rejected with exit code 4 and goes to quarantine; bad lines are rejected one by one and listed; exact duplicates are dropped. Step 3, read and plan as in lesson 78; with the dry-run option the job stops here and reports. Step 4, the journal gets the entry started, then the writes go out in batches; ServiceClient waits when throttled; if it is still throttled the journal gets throttled and the exit code is 3, and the file stays in the inbox for the next scheduled run. Step 5, the journal gets completed with the summary, the run report is written, and the exit code is 0 if clean or 1 if lines need a person; the file goes to the archive. Exit code 2 means configuration, connection or another active run; the file stays in the inbox. Below, the Python reconciliation reads the same file and asks Dataverse independently whether any work order is behind the feed.
svg.text: 02:00, nobody watching: every exit has a place for the file and someone who reacts
journal: completed + summary; run report (counts, IDs, reasons)
exit 0 clean | exit 1 lines need a person
Exit code → where the file goes → who reacts
Independent check: python -m cedar_service.reconcile <the same file>
Another language, the Web API, another identity, a different question: is any work order BEHIND what the feed last said?
Further along is fine (late lines, work done in the app). Exit 1 when something is behind or ambiguous.
The job runs as the application user FieldLink Sync with a certificate; on the job host it refuses to run as a person.
